vulnerability.description: Sandbox escape in notevil and argencoders-notevil

relatedVulnerabilities.description: This affects all versions of package notevil; all versions of package argencoders-notevil. It is vulnerable to Sandbox Escape leading to Prototype pollution. The package fails to restrict access to the main context, allowing an attacker to add or modify an object's prototype. **Note:** This vulnerability derives from an incomplete fix in [SNYK-JS-NOTEVIL-608878](https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-NOTEVIL-608878).

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: A QUIC server that rejects a stream opened by the peer may retain that stream's state for the lifetime of the connection if the peer resets the stream before the rejection is signalled, even though the peer's stream credit is returned.  Impact summary: A remote client that completes a QUIC handshake can repeatedly open and reset streams, causing server memory to grow without bound until the process runs out of memory and every connection on it is lost. This is a Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-401: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime  Description: QUIC servers track each stream the peer opens. When the incoming stream policy rejects a stream, OpenSSL schedules a STOP_SENDING frame, marks the stream deleted and returns the peer's stream credit. A deleted stream is collected only once its receive part is fully drained, which for a rejected stream means the STOP_SENDING has been acknowledged. If the peer sends RESET_STREAM first, the reset cancels the pending STOP_SENDING, so it is never sent or acknowledged and the stream is never collected.  The default configuration reaches this path. Once a connection has a default stream, meaning the application has read from or written to the connection as the tutorial server does, the effective incoming stream policy rejects streams the application does not accept. Applications that set the REJECT policy explicitly are affected too.  Each retained stream costs about 300 bytes, and the peer's stream credit window paces how quickly they accumulate. A client that keeps the connection open and keeps opening and resetting streams grows server memory without bound. The severity is Low because growth is slow, needs a long-lived connection, and causes no memory corruption or disclosure.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: hbs: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Externally-Accessible File or Directory and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

relatedVulnerabilities.description: The npm hbs package is an Express view engine wrapper for Handlebars. Depending on usage, users of hbs may be vulnerable to a file disclosure vulnerability. There is currently no patch for this vulnerability. hbs mixes pure template data with engine configuration options through the Express render API. By overwriting internal configuration options a file disclosure vulnerability may be triggered in downstream applications. For an example PoC see the referenced GHSL-2021-020.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: Setting an AES-GCM-SIV IV shorter than the expected nonce length via EVP_CipherInit_ex() may trigger a heap out-of-bounds read. Supplying a longer IV is silently truncated instead of rejected.  Impact summary: An application passing a caller-supplied IV of the wrong length may crash or read beyond its buffer. Because trailing IV bytes are ignored, an attacker who knows one message and tag may forge messages under a different IV.  CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read  Description: AES-GCM-SIV copies the caller-supplied IV or nonce into its internal state using a copy whose length is taken from the expected nonce size rather than from the length the caller actually provided. When the caller passes a shorter IV, the copy reads past the end of the caller's buffer; AddressSanitizer confirms a heap out-of-bounds read reached through EVP_CipherInit_ex() into ossl_aes_gcm_siv_init(). When the caller passes a longer IV, the implementation silently discards the trailing bytes instead of rejecting the length.  The truncation breaks the binding between the IV and the computed authentication tag. An attacker who has observed a message and its tag under one IV can produce a message and tag that verify under a different IV whose first bytes match, since the surplus bytes never influence the computation. The message itself is unchanged, so this is a failure of IV commitment rather than a classic existential forgery.  Only applications that call EVP_CipherInit_ex() (or the equivalent provider cipher initialization) with an IV length other than the standard 12 bytes for AES-GCM-SIV are affected. The severity is limited because the out-of-bounds read is small and attacker-controlled only in length, and the forgery requires an unusual IV length choice by the application.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules are not affected by this issue, as AES-GCM-SIV is not an approved algorithm.

vulnerability.description: A flaw was found in the libstdc++ component of GCC. An attacker who can provide an excessively large element count to a boolean vector (std::vector<bool>) constructor can trigger an integer wrap during internal memory calculations. This issue leaves the container in an inconsistent state, leading to out-of-bounds memory access and resulting in an application crash or a Denial of Service (DoS) during subsequent operations.

vulnerability.description: A flaw was found in GCC. When an application calls the erase_if function on a binary heap priority queue in libstdc++, the library reallocates storage but fails to update its internal entry pointer. An attacker capable of triggering this operation can exploit this use-after-free condition, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) via an application crash or potential memory corruption.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: Encrypting a CMS message to an EC certificate whose group order is 1 may cause CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() to loop indefinitely.  Impact summary: An attacker able to supply the recipient certificate to an application performing CMS encryption can cause that application to loop indefinitely, consuming CPU and resulting in Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')  Description: CMS_encrypt() and CMS_encrypt_ex() encrypt a message to one or more recipient certificates and, for an EC recipient, generate an ephemeral key in the recipient's group. If the certificate declares a group order of 1, random scalar generation can only produce zero. The key generation routine then retries without limit while waiting for a nonzero private scalar, so the call never returns.  The OpenSSL TLS and QUIC implementations do not use this path. An application is exposed only if it calls CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() with a recipient certificate whose EC parameters are attacker-controlled. Certificates with normal EC group orders do not trigger the loop.  OpenSSL 4.0 and later reject unknown explicit EC groups in default builds. These versions are affected only when configured with the enable-ec_explicit_curves option.  The result is a hang that consumes a CPU core until the process is interrupted, a Denial of Service. The severity is Low because the attacker must supply the recipient certificate and the application must choose to encrypt to it; ordinary CMS encryption to trusted recipients is unaffected.  The fix makes EC key generation fail when the group has no valid nonzero private scalar, instead of retrying indefinitely.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules in 4.1, 4.0, 3.5 and 3.0 are not affected. The FIPS provider does not support arbitrary explicit EC domain parameters, so an order-1 group is rejected during key import before the vulnerable key generation path is reached.

vulnerability.description: Glob: AbortSignal cancellation bypass allows post-timeout filesystem traversal

relatedVulnerabilities.description: Glob matches files using patterns the shell uses. From 9.0.0 until 14.0.2, abort branches in src/walker.ts, including GlobUtil.walkCB(), GlobUtil.walkCB2(), GlobUtil.walkCBSync(), and GlobUtil.walkCB2Sync(), invoke the callbacks without returning. After AbortSignal or AbortSignal.timeout() rejects or emits an error, execution can continue into processor.processPatterns(), readdirCB(), and recursive traversal. The issue affects glob() and globStream() when applications expose attacker-influenced patterns or directory trees and rely on cancellation as a traversal budget. Repeated timed-out requests can stack background filesystem operations and CPU work, degrading worker throughput or service availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed. This issue is fixed in 14.0.2.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: Calling EVP_EncodeBlock() with an input length close to INT_MAX may overflow the calculation of the encoded output size and write past the end of the caller-supplied output buffer.  Impact summary: No path by which an attacker can trigger this has been identified. An application that passes an input length near INT_MAX to EVP_EncodeBlock() could suffer a heap buffer overflow, crashing or corrupting its own memory, but it must itself supply such a length.  CWE: CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound  Description: EVP_EncodeBlock() base64-encodes a buffer of a caller-supplied length into an output buffer that the caller allocates. The caller is expected to reserve 4*((len+2)/3)+1 bytes. For input lengths close to INT_MAX, the arithmetic that computes the encoded length overflows a signed integer, so the function writes more data than the documented output size. The result is a heap buffer overflow in the calling process.  Reaching this requires an application to pass an input length near INT_MAX to EVP_EncodeBlock(). OpenSSL's TLS, QUIC and CMS implementations never encode buffers of that size, and the command line tools cannot practically be made to do so: the limits on reading a proxy password from a file and on bignum sizes prevent it. An application that accepts an attacker-controlled length and forwards it to EVP_EncodeBlock() without its own bound check is exposed.  The severity is Low because no attacker-controlled path to the overflow is known. The caller must already hold a buffer of about two gigabytes before the defect can be reached.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: Converting crafted ISO-2022-CN-EXT input to UTF-8 character encoding, in the GNU C Library version 2.2 through 2.44 may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When the ISO-2022-CN-EXT decoder encounters an invalid input byte sequence like '\x0e' it ends up advancing the pointer tracking the read buffer position twice.  If this sequence is at the end of the input buffer, the decoder may then end up reading past the bounds of the input buffer.  To exploit this, the input and encoding needs to be attacker controlled.

vulnerability.description: Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character encoding, in the GNU C Library version 2.3.3 and later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When converting from UCS-4, these encoders may encounter a combining base such as U+00E6 and jump ahead by 4 bytes to check the next UCS-4 code point.  The check for end of buffer however does not account for this, which may result in a buffer overread if the following code point has less than 4 bytes remaining.  Exploitation of this bug not only requires attacker control of input and encoding, but also strict control over layout of the input in memory.

vulnerability.description: minimatch has potential denial of service via globparts amplification

relatedVulnerabilities.description: minimatch is a minimal matching utility for converting glob expressions into JavaScript RegExp objects. Starting in 7.0.0 and prior to 11.0.1, src/index.ts implements firstPhasePreProcess() so that, at optimizationLevel 2 or higher, it repeatedly expands attacker-controlled **/.. pattern segments inside a fixpoint loop, allowing generated globParts entries to be processed and expanded again. secondPhasePreProcess() then compares the expanded entries pairwise, so a short malicious glob can cause excessive CPU and memory consumption during pattern compilation. This issue is fixed in version 11.0.1.

vulnerability.description: uuid: Missing buffer bounds check in v3/v5/v6 when buf is provided

relatedVulnerabilities.description: uuid is for the creation of RFC9562 (formerly RFC4122) UUIDs. Prior to 14.0.0, v3, v5, and v6 accept external output buffers but do not reject out-of-range writes (small buf or large offset). This allows silent partial writes into caller-provided buffers. This vulnerability is fixed in 14.0.0.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: A retransmitted QUIC CRYPTO frame can release packet storage while the TLS record layer retains a direct pointer into that storage causing use after free.  Impact summary: A malicious QUIC server can cause a heap-use-after-free read in the OpenSSL QUIC client. The server can also identify one allocator-adjacent byte through the client's protected Handshake response.  CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free  Description: During CRYPTO stream processing, a pointer into the first frame's memory on the stream is lent to the TLS handshake processing. The memory must remain stable until it is processed and released. However the processing of retransmitted CRYPTO frames could release the memory if the retransmitted frame fully overlapped the existing frame. This then causes use-after-free read when the TLS handshake processing continues.  The use-after-free read can lead to a Denial-of-Service of the client application or a minor leak of information about the heap memory contents that might be overwritten with other data, subsequently allocated by the application, to the peer.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS module is not affected as the QUIC implementation is outside of the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: The gettext family of functions in the GNU C Library version 2.0 and later accept LANGUAGE environment variable entries that contain '/' or that are equal to "..", unless the program is setuid or setgid (AT_SECURE).  An attacker who can set LANGUAGE in the environment of a program that uses gettext can make it load a message catalog (.mo file) from an arbitrary location in the file system.  A crafted .mo file can crash the program through out-of-range offsets, or supply translations whose format directives do not match the arguments passed by the program.  That causes undefined behaviour in the printf family of functions and may allow arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the program.  The safety of message catalogs relies on them being installed in trusted, read-only locations, and the directory traversal bypasses this.  The fix for CVE-2014-0475 rejects ".." path components in locale names passed to setlocale or taken from the LC_ALL, LC_* and LANG environment variables.  gettext reads LANGUAGE directly and appends each colon-separated entry to the message catalog directory, so that fix did not cover LANGUAGE.  LANGUAGE is only used when the LC_MESSAGES locale is not "C", "C.<encoding>" or "POSIX", so the attacker must also be able to select another installed locale, for example through LANG or LC_ALL. vulnerability.description: Issue summary: The AES-GCM-SIV implementation treats a zero-length Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) update as a reset of all the AAD supplied so far, instead of leaving the AAD unchanged. An application that supplies its AAD in several fragments, one of which is empty, therefore produces or verifies messages whose authentication tag does not cover the AAD supplied before the empty fragment.  Impact summary: Data an application intended to authenticate alongside a message is silently left unauthenticated. An attacker can forge the AAD of such a message.  CWE: CWE-325: Missing Cryptographic Step  Description: An application passing AAD in multiple chunks of which some have zero length will have the previous AAD chunks effectively unauthenticated. Also, on context re-initialisation, the AAD was not reset, which meant that any AAD accumulated from the previous context usage were also included in the AAD of the new message.  The fix makes a zero-length AAD update a no-op and clears any accumulated AAD whenever the context is re-initialised with a key or a nonce. A re-initialisation that only changes parameters keeps the AAD.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules are not affected, as AES-GCM-SIV is not a FIPS approved algorithm and is implemented only in the default provider, outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: file-type affected by infinite loop in ASF parser on malformed input with zero-size sub-header

relatedVulnerabilities.description: file-type detects the file type of a file, stream, or data. Prior to 21.3.1, a denial of service vulnerability exists in the ASF (WMV/WMA) file type detection parser. When parsing a crafted input where an ASF sub-header has a size field of zero, the parser enters an infinite loop. The payload value becomes negative (-24), causing tokenizer.ignore(payload) to move the read position backwards, so the same sub-header is read repeatedly forever. Any application that uses file-type to detect the type of untrusted/attacker-controlled input is affected. An attacker can stall the Node.js event loop with a 55-byte payload. Fixed in version 21.3.1.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: A DANE-enabled TLS client may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer when processing an unusual combination of certificate and TLSA records.  Impact summary: The impact is limited to a client crash (potential Denial of Service).  CWE: CWE-476: NULL Pointer Dereference  Description: A DANE-enabled TLS client that supports TLSA records with at least one of the PKIX-TA(0) or PKIX-EE(1) usages alongside the DANE-TA(2) usage may crash by dereferencing a NULL pointer if the server claims a trusted CA's certificate to be its end-entity certificate and has an unusual mix of associated TLSA records.  DANE SMTP clients should not be affected since only the DANE-TA(2) and DANE-EE(3) TLSA record usages are specified applicable in SMTP.  For example, the Postfix MTA is not affected, while the Exim MTA does not at present use OpenSSL's DANE implementation.  Use of DANE in validation of RFC7250 raw public keys (RPKs) is also unaffected, as these only use DANE-EE(3) TLSA records.  Only applications that support combining the DANE PKI with a traditional PKI are potentially affected.  A DANE-enabled browser or similar, that uses OpenSSL's DANE API could be affected.  FIPS impact: no The DANE API is outside the FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: Converting crafted CP949 input to UTF-8 character encoding and ignoring invalid characters, in the GNU C Library version 2.1 or later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When the CP949 decoder encounters an invalid input byte sequence like '\xa2\xe8' it ends up advancing the pointer tracking the read buffer position twice.  If //IGNORE is set on the destination encoding and this sequence is at the end of the input buffer, the decoder may then end up reading past the bounds of the input buffer.  To exploit this, the target iconv function needs to set //IGNORE on the destination of the conversion and the input and encoding needs to be attacker controlled.

vulnerability.description: The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched.  The names already rewritten are freed, but their pointers stay in the result vector, and the error path frees them again with globfree.  The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: QUIC, when performing automated peer detection, may allow uninitialized stack data to leak into the received address which is then used as the destination for outgoing packets.  Impact summary: Applications using QUIC's automated peer detection mechanism may receive an invalid address, leading to connection loss and disclosure of uninitialized stack data to an attacker observing the outgoing network traffic.  CWE: CWE-457 (Use of Uninitialized Variable)  Description: The OpenSSL QUIC stack contains a feature in which, when using an already connected socket, it will auto-detect the peer address during the SSL handshake.  This feature uses the getpeername() function, passing a buffer of sufficient length to hold any supported address family, but passes a buffer length that is only sized such that larger addresses, such as IPv6, cannot be retrieved. The getpeername() function however, still returns the full address length, which is accepted as the valid input buffer length, leading to the address buffer containing uninitialized stack data instead of the actual peer address. The invalid peer address is then used as destination for the outgoing packets which leads to a connectivity breakage and a leakage of the uninitialized stack data to passive network observers.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules in 4.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, and 3.0 are not affected by this CVE as the affected protocol is not implemented in the FIPS module.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: Receiving crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments may cause OpenSSL to allocate a full message-length reassembly buffer for each buffered message, so a small amount of wire data consumes a large amount of memory.  Impact summary: A remote attacker can send a few small crafted DTLS handshake fragments to make a DTLS server or client allocate well over a megabyte of memory per connection, which may lead to memory exhaustion and Denial of Service if many connections are made.  CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling  Description: DTLS handshake messages can arrive out of order and fragmented, so OpenSSL buffers fragments of up to ten out-of-sequence messages until reassembly is possible. When the first fragment of a new message arrives, OpenSSL allocates a buffer sized to the full message length declared in the fragment header, plus a reassembly bitmap, instead of storing only the bytes actually received. The declared length is capped by the maximum certificate list size, 128KB by default, and that cap applies to every handshake message type rather than only to Certificate messages.  Only DTLS endpoints reach this code. TLS, QUIC and applications that do not use DTLS are unaffected. An attacker sends fragments that declare a large message length but carry almost no data, using up to ten distinct message sequence numbers.  A single connection can then hold roughly 1.4MB of buffers from about 156 bytes on the wire. Because the number of buffered messages is capped, memory exhaustion requires many connections or many peers, which is why the severity is Low.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: Calling the wide scanf family of functions (swscanf, fwscanf, wscanf, vswscanf, vfwscanf and vwscanf) with a %s or %[ conversion without the 'l' length modifier in the GNU C Library version 2.2 to version 2.44 writes an extra null byte one past the end of the destination array when the converted multibyte string and its terminating null byte exactly fill that array.  These conversions store each wide input character into the caller's char array as a multibyte sequence.  The conversion ends with the sequence that returns to the initial shift state, which also stores the terminating null byte, and the functions then append a second null byte.  A destination sized for the converted string and one terminator, as the C standard requires the caller to provide, is therefore written one byte past its end.  The out-of-bounds byte is always a null byte, which may corrupt adjacent data or crash the process.  An attacker who supplies the input can trigger the overflow with a string whose converted length exactly fills the destination.  The narrow scanf functions, the %ls and %l[ conversions into a wchar_t array, and the 'a' and 'm' allocation modifiers are not affected, and storing a wide scanf conversion into a narrow char array is uncommon.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: A server configured with the Suite B certificate flag through SSL_CTX_set_cert_flags() and with TLS 1.3 enabled may read past the end of a fixed group list when it processes a ClientHello whose supported_groups and key_share contain no Suite B group.  Impact summary: A remote client can send a ClientHello that makes the server read past the end of a static array. The values read are never returned to the client, so no memory is disclosed; on builds with sanitizers or hardened allocators the read may crash the process, causing Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read  Description: When the Suite B certificate flag is set, OpenSSL restricts the accepted groups to P-256 and P-384 by substituting a fixed two-element list for the configured group list. The tuple machinery used for key-share selection was not updated for this substitution: tls1_get_group_tuples() still returns the configured tuples, which by default describe eight groups. The server-side walk in tls_parse_ctos_key_share() then advances through the two-element list using those tuple counts without checking the cumulative offset against the number of groups present.  Only applications that call SSL_CTX_set_cert_flags() with SSL_CERT_FLAG_SUITEB_128_LOS and leave TLS 1.3 enabled are affected. The openssl s_server -suiteB_128 option sets an X.509 verification parameter instead, so the stock command line server is not vulnerable. Default configurations do not reach this code.  A client that offers only groups outside the Suite B set, such as X25519, forces every tuple to be walked and the read to run past the array. The bytes read are compared against client group IDs and never sent back, so no memory is disclosed. On builds with address sanitizers or hardened allocators the read can abort the process; in ordinary release builds it reads a few bytes of adjacent constant data.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

An attacker capable of inducing repeated write failures in an affected service can trigger a buffer overflow, potentially resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption.

vulnerability.description: Issue summary: When an application passes a stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() to add entries to, and reading fails, OpenSSL frees every entry in the stack, both the old ones and any new ones, but leaves them in the stack.  Impact summary: An application that passes an existing stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() and keeps using it after a failed read may use memory that was already freed. This can cause a crash or, in principle, memory corruption. Malformed PEM data can make the read fail, but only applications that pass an existing stack are affected, and OpenSSL itself does not do this.  CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free  Description: PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() reads certificates, CRLs and private keys from PEM data and adds them to a stack of X509_INFO structures. If the application passes a stack that is not NULL, the function adds the new entries to it and must leave the entries that are already there unchanged.  If reading fails, the function frees every entry in the stack. This includes the entries that were there before the call, and the entries added by the call. It does not remove these entries from the stack, so the stack keeps pointers to freed memory. The failure can happen at any point, even before any entry was added. A PEM item with invalid content is enough.  This also happens if the stack was empty: entries added before the failure are freed but stay in the stack.  An application that then reads or frees the stack will use memory that was already freed. This can crash the application or, in principle, corrupt memory.  Only applications that pass a stack that is not NULL are affected. OpenSSL itself never does this. Its own callers, including the code that TLS uses to load CA certificates, always pass NULL. When the stack is NULL, the function frees only the entries that it created itself, which is safe. We expect that very few applications pass an existing stack. An attacker can make the read fail with malformed PEM data, but cannot make an application pass an existing stack.  The same problem affects PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio(), PEM_X509_INFO_read() and PEM_X509_INFO_read_ex(), which use the same code. OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 have only the first two of these functions.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

vulnerability.description: The regcomp and regexec functions in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to version 2.44 may read freed memory and free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while a regular expression is compiled or matched.  The re_dfa_add_node (the NFA node table) and build_range_exp (bracket ranges) grow several arrays with consecutive realloc calls and store the new pointers only after all of them succeed.  When a later call fails, the pattern buffer keeps pointers to blocks that were already freed, and the error cleanup frees them again.  In regexec, the back-reference cache (match_ctx_add_entry) frees its array when a realloc fails but keeps the pointer, which is freed again on the error path.  An attacker does not need to supply a crafted regular expression: patterns large enough to grow these arrays are common.  The failure has to hit a specific allocation, though, so the issue can only be reached when the system is already under memory pressure.  An attacker who supplies the pattern or the subject string has little control over which allocation fails, so the expected impact is a crash of the process.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

vulnerability.description: A flaw was found in GCC. An out-of-bounds memory access vulnerability exists in the libstdc++ parallel search implementation due to an undersized internal buffer. A local attacker can exploit this flaw by providing crafted search data to an application compiled with parallel mode, causing the process to crash and leading to a Denial of Service (DoS).

vulnerability.description: @tootallnate/once vulnerable to Incorrect Control Flow Scoping

relatedVulnerabilities.description: Versions of the package @tootallnate/once before 3.0.1 are vulnerable to Incorrect Control Flow Scoping in promise resolving when AbortSignal option is used. The Promise remains in a permanently pending state after the signal is aborted, causing any await or .then() usage to hang indefinitely. This can cause a control-flow leak that can lead to stalled requests, blocked workers, or degraded application availability.

vulnerability.description: A flaw was found in GCC libstdc++. When an application extracts data into a bitset from a wide-character stream, internal stack memory allocation fails to properly account for character size and alignment. An attacker capable of supplying crafted input to an affected application could trigger a stack-based buffer overflow leading denial of service (DoS).
